conversation.content:
Hello there, Mama. My name is Maya; I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician on the team. I’m here today simply to check in on how things have been feeling for you since your baby arrived. We use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale – or EPDS – which helps us pick up on any signs of depression, anxiety, or distress that can sometimes creep up in the weeks after birth.  

This is a routine screen we offer all new moms; your answers stay confidential within your medical record and will only be shared with other members of your care team if you need extra support. There are no right or wrong answers – just whatever feels true for you right now. I’ll ask you ten gentle questions about the past seven days, and we’ll go at whatever pace feels comfortable.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can start with the first question:  

Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has even pleasant moments felt kind of flat or “meh”?

[soft shrug, eyes a little misty]  
I still smile sometimes—like when she grips my finger—but it doesn’t feel as bright as before. It’s more… muted, I guess. Things I used to get excited about feel kind of “meh,” and I have to remind myself to enjoy them rather than just naturally feeling it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod, small half-smile]  
Yeah, I’ve laughed a little—mostly at silly stuff my husband does or the faces the baby makes—but it feels kind of forced or not as strong as it used to. Like I can see something’s funny, but the laugh doesn’t bubble up the same way.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[glances down, smoothing the blanket]  
Not really. I mean, I tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like taking her for a walk or having coffee with a friend—but when I think about them, it just feels kind of flat. I go through the motions hoping the enjoyment will kick in, but most times it doesn’t.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[sighs, voice quiet]  
Yeah… a few times. Like if she’s fussy and won’t settle, I catch myself thinking maybe I’m not doing something right or I’m missing some “mom instinct” everyone else seems to have. I know logically babies just cry, but the thought still pops up that it’s my fault somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping the edge of the blanket around my fingers]  
Sometimes, yeah. Out of nowhere I’ll get this fluttery feeling—like, is she breathing okay, am I holding her right, what if I missed something? It usually passes pretty quick once I check on her or distract myself, but it definitely shows up without a real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[exhales slowly]  
Not really panicked… more like a sudden knot in my stomach when I imagine something bad happening to her. My heart races for a minute, then I take a few deep breaths and it fades. It’s unsettling, but I haven’t had a full-blown “scared” spell.
Things have been getting on top of me

[soft laugh, eyes tired]  
Yeah, some days it feels like the laundry and bottles and night feeds just pile up, and I think, “How am I going to get through all this?” I manage—eventually—but it’s like I’m wading through mud to finish even small tasks.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I mean, I feel a bit down sometimes, but I can still fall asleep okay. Once the baby’s settled, I drift off—maybe takes a little longer if I’m replaying the day in my head, but nothing too bad.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes glaze a little]  
Yeah… I’ve had moments where it just feels heavy, like a cloud sitting on me. Not all day, but it comes and goes, especially when I’m alone with her and the house is quiet. I’ll just feel weepy and wonder why I can’t snap out of it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quiet voice, dabbing at my eyes with the edge of my sleeve]  
A couple of times this week. It’s not constant, but when everything feels piled up—her crying, the mess, my own tiredness—the tears just come. I usually cry for a minute or two, wipe my face, and keep going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed or tearful, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of her.

You've shared that while you can still smile at your baby's tiny grip, the joy often feels muted, and plans that once excited you now seem flat. You've noticed yourself tearing up, feeling a heavy cloud settle in quiet moments, and worrying about being enough for her. Laughing feels forced, tasks feel like wading through mud, and self-blame creeps in when she fusses. You've also described sudden fluttery worries about her safety, but you're relieved these pass quickly and you've never had thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient admits recurring self-blame "a few times" tied to baby fussiness, matching "Yes, some of the time" (2 points)</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, intrusive worry that arises "out of nowhere" multiple times, matching the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily overwhelm with tasks piling up and effortful coping, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Her description of a "heavy cloud," weepiness, and inability to "snap out of it" indicates sadness occurring "quite often" though not continuously.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 15 places you above the 13 threshold indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. Key symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest or pleasure (Q2 score 3), inappropriate guilt (Q3 score 2), low mood (Q8 score 2), and functional difficulty (Q6 score 2). Combined with frequent worry and mild physiologic anxiety, these suggest clinically significant distress requiring prompt follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next week
2. Discuss possibility of counseling such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> tailored for postpartum women
3. Re-screen EPDS in two weeks to track changes after support measures are in place
4. Share Edinburgh score with your midwife or obstetrician so the whole team is aware
5. Ask partners or family to help with overnight feeds and household tasks to protect sleep and reduce <sym>stress</sym>
6. Schedule brief daily outdoor walks; gentle exercise can lift mood and reduce <sym>anxiety</sym>
7. Keep emergency numbers handy: local 24-h crisis line, your maternity unit triage, and a trusted friend you can call day or night
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) interview, self-report + behavioral observation, 2 wks postpartum.

Symptoms endorsed (≥ several days per week):
- Anhedonia / diminished pleasure (Q2)
- Self-blame / inappropriate guilt (Q3)
- Persistent worry / intrusive “what-if” thoughts (Q4)
- Episodic dysphoria, tearfulness (Q8, Q9)
- Feeling overwhelmed / “wading through mud” to complete tasks (Q6)
- Fleeting physiologic anxiety (racing heart, stomach knot) without full panic (Q4, Q5)

Sleep: Onset occasionally prolonged by rumination; baby-driven interruptions only (Q7).

Safety: Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (Q10); no protective-plan concerns voiced.

Pattern: Sub-syndromal depressive and anxious symptoms impacting daily functioning; no frank major depressive or panic episodes to date.

Screening significance: Elevated risk for postpartum depression ± anxiety; score not yet totaled—recommend formal EPDS scoring and follow-up within 1–2 weeks, psychoeducation, support-system review.
